blocks.title: Key terms
items: 'Federation' comes from the Latin word 'foedus', which means 'treaty' or 'agreement'.
Units of a federation have different names: states (USA), cantons (Switzerland), provinces (Canada), republics (Russia).
Federation by integration ('coming together'): weak independent states join to form a strong union — example USA (1787).
Federation by disintegration ('holding together'): a big unitary state gives autonomy to its provinces and becomes a federation — example Canada (1867). India also followed this route.
USA is the first and oldest federation (formed 1787 after the American Revolution 1775–83); it had 13 states originally and has 50 now.
Canada (1867) had 4 provinces originally and has 10 now.

Confederation: a loose, voluntary association of sovereign states made by an agreement between governments; members keep their sovereignty and can leave it. Example: the USA under the Articles of Confederation (before 1787).
Difference: in a federation the central government acts directly on citizens; in a confederation it acts only through the member governments.
Judicial review (courts checking laws against the Constitution) is a symbol of a federal government, because courts settle disputes between the levels.
Separation of powers between legislature, executive and judiciary is NOT what makes a system federal — federalism is about division of power between levels of government.
Drawback of heavy centralisation in a diverse country: uniform policies may ignore local needs and may slow down regional policy innovation.

sections.heading: How India became a 'Union of States'

items: Why India chose federalism: the large size of the country and its socio-cultural diversity. Federalism gives efficient government and also balances national unity with regional autonomy.
The word 'federation' is not used anywhere in the Constitution. Article 1 calls India a 'Union of States'. The Preamble also does not call India federal.

Ambedkar's two reasons for 'Union of States' instead of 'Federation of States': (1) the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among the states, unlike the American federation; (2) the states have no right to secede (leave) from the federation. The Union is indestructible.
Ambedkar explained this when he moved the Draft Constitution in the Constituent Assembly on 4 November 1948.
India follows the Canadian model, not the American model. The Canadian model creates a very strong Centre.

India resembles Canada in 3 ways: (1) formation by disintegration; (2) use of the term 'Union' (Canada is also called a Union); (3) centralising tendency (more powers to the Centre). Residuary powers in Canada are with the Centre too — NOT with the provinces.
From the Canadian Constitution India borrowed 'federation with a strong Centre' and 'residuary powers with the Centre'.

Government of India Act, 1935: gave the scheme of distribution of powers and the three lists (Federal, Provincial, Concurrent). It first introduced a federal structure with provincial autonomy. Under it residuary powers were given to the Governor-General (Viceroy).
Under the 1935 Act the provinces were never sovereign states; the Act laid the basis of Indian federalism. So the Indian Union is not a compact (agreement) between states that can be broken.

India is called 'an indestructible Union of destructible states'. This is because Parliament can change the area, boundary or name of any state by an ordinary law under Article 3, by a simple majority, without the state's consent. The USA is 'an indestructible Union of indestructible states', because the US Congress cannot change a state's boundary without that state's consent.
No state has a constitutional right to secede unilaterally from the Union.

sections.heading: Federal features and unitary features of India

head: Federal feature
What it means
rows: Union at the Centre and states at the periphery; each is sovereign (supreme) in the field given to it by the Constitution. Union: defence, foreign affairs, currency, communication. States: public order, agriculture, health, local government.
Lengthiest written Constitution in the world; it lays down the powers and limits of both Centre and states.

Seventh Schedule: Union List 98 subjects (originally 97), State List 59 (originally 66), Concurrent List 52 (originally 47). On a Concurrent subject, Central law prevails in a conflict. Residuary subjects go to the Centre.
Highest law of the land; laws of Centre and states that break it can be struck down by the Supreme Court or High Courts (judicial review).
Provisions on the federal structure (Centre–state relations, judiciary) need a special majority of Parliament and approval by half of the state legislatures.
Headed by the Supreme Court; protects the Constitution and settles disputes between Centre and states or between states (Article 131 — original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, not High Courts).
Rajya Sabha represents the states and maintains federal equilibrium (balance) by protecting state interests; Lok Sabha represents the people as a whole.
blocks.title: 7 federal features (Laxmikanth)

head: Unitary (non-federal) feature
What it means
Article / comparison
rows: The Union List has more subjects than the State List, and the important subjects (like defence) are in the Union List. On a Concurrent List subject, a Central law prevails over a state law. Residuary powers (subjects not in any list) are with the Centre; in the USA they are with the states
Parliament alone can change the area, boundary or name of a state, by a simple majority, without the state's consent
One Constitution for Centre and states; only exception was the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir (till 2019). J&K no longer has a separate constitution
Most of it can be amended by Parliament alone; only the Centre (Parliament) can start an amendment. In USA states can also propose amendments
Rajya Sabha seats are based on population: from 1 (e.g. Sikkim) to 31 (Uttar Pradesh). The US Senate gives 2 seats to every state (100 members)
National, state and financial emergencies make the Centre all-powerful; the federal structure becomes unitary WITHOUT any formal amendment
Only Indian citizenship, like Canada. USA and Australia have dual citizenship
One system of courts (Supreme Court at top, High Courts below) enforces both Central and state laws. USA has a double system of courts

The Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS) and Indian Forest Service (IFoS) serve both the Centre and the states. The Centre recruits and trains these officers and has final control over them. So they go against the federal principle

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audits the accounts of both the Centre and the states. But the President appoints and removes the CAG without consulting the states, so this limits the states' financial freedom
Parliament can make laws on a State List subject if Rajya Sabha passes a resolution in the national interest — even when there is NO emergency
Appointed by the President, holds office during the President's pleasure, acts as agent of the Centre. India followed the Canadian system; the USA has elected state heads
Election Commission conducts elections to Centre and states, but is formed by the President; states have no say
Governor can reserve state bills for the President, who can withhold assent again and again — an absolute veto. Seen as an example of Central control over states
blocks.title: 14 unitary features (Laxmikanth)
Quick points
items: These are usually NOT counted among the main federal features (in exam options): allocation of financial resources, the office of the Governor, the CAG, collective responsibility, All-India Services, single citizenship and integrated judiciary.
Limits on the sovereignty of Indian Parliament: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, federalism and a written Constitution.
Judicial power is NOT divided between Centre and states (India has an integrated judiciary); legislative, executive and financial powers are divided.
A district judge applying both a Central Act and a state Act on the same day shows integrated judiciary.
Doctrine of paramountcy (also called repugnancy — when a state law conflicts with a Union law): on a Concurrent List subject, the Union law prevails over the conflicting state law (Article 254).
During an emergency India is described as 'unitary'.

In 'which is a federal feature' questions: the President taking over a state's government in an emergency, and Parliament's exclusive residuary power, are signs of a strong Centre (unitary). Only the division of power through the three lists is a purely federal feature.
The Finance Commission keeps financial balance between Union and states; the Constitution gives more financial powers to the Union.
For the Seventh Schedule, Article 249 and the amendments that moved subjects between lists, see the Legislative relations card.

blocks.title: Nature and trends
items: Common description: 'federal in form but unitary in spirit' — all usual federal features exist, plus many unitary features that favour the Centre. Also called 'unitary with federal features' / quasi-federal.
Indian federalism is a compromise between (1) state autonomy under the normal division of powers and (2) national integrity and a strong Union in exceptional situations.

Signs of federal spirit: territorial disputes (Belgaum: Maharashtra–Karnataka); river water disputes (Cauvery: Karnataka–Tamil Nadu); rise of regional parties in states like Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu; new states (Mizoram, Jharkhand, Telangana); demand for more grants; states asserting autonomy; Supreme Court limits on Article 356. (Parliament legislating on a State subject during emergency is NOT a sign of federal spirit.)
Cooperative federalism: Centre and states work together. It got new importance after NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission; NITI Aayog's Governing Council includes Chief Ministers.
Competitive federalism: states compete for investment and growth; it gained importance after the 1991 economic reforms.
Relations between Centre and states are vertical; relations among states are horizontal.
The term 'fiscal federalism' was first used by Richard Musgrave in 1959.
Coalition governments tend to strengthen federalism, because a coalition at the Centre depends on regional parties and so listens to regional demands.

at_a_glance: Seventh Schedule: Union List (List I), State List (List II), Concurrent List (List III)

blocks.text: Laxmikanth splits Centre–State legislative relations into four parts: (1) territorial extent of laws, (2) distribution of subjects, (3) Parliament making laws in the State field, and (4) the Centre's control over State laws. blocks.title: Territorial extent — Art 245
head: Who
Can make laws for
Outside its territory?
rows: The whole or any part of the territory of India (States, Union Territories and any other area included in India)

Yes. Only Parliament can make extra-territorial laws (laws that apply outside India). They apply to Indian citizens and their property anywhere in the world. Art 245(2): a law of Parliament is NOT invalid merely because it operates outside India.
The whole or any part of that State only

Normally no. Exception: a State law can reach outside the State if there is a sufficient nexus (real connection) between the State and the object of the law. This is called the doctrine of territorial nexus.

For Puducherry, only when its Assembly is suspended or dissolved.
Governor of a State can direct that an Act of Parliament shall not apply to a Scheduled Area (Fifth Schedule area) in the State, or shall apply with changes.
Governor of Assam can do the same for tribal areas (autonomous districts) in Assam; the President has this power for tribal areas in Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram (Sixth Schedule).

blocks.title: Other rules in Art 246, 246A and 247
items: Order of priority (predominance) when Lists overlap: the Union List comes first, then the Concurrent List, then the State List. This is because Art 246 makes the State List 'subject to' both other Lists.

Art 246(4): Parliament can make laws on ANY matter, even a State List matter, for a part of India not included in a State — that is, Union Territories (for example, a police law for a Union Territory without a legislature is valid).

Art 246A (added by the 101st Amendment, 2016): Parliament AND State Legislatures both can make laws on Goods and Services Tax (GST). But only Parliament can make laws on GST on inter-state supplies (supply in the course of inter-state trade). See cs-financial for GST details.
Art 247: Parliament may set up additional courts for better administration of laws made by Parliament on Union List matters.

Logic of the split: subjects of national importance that need one uniform law go to the Union List; regional and local subjects go to the State List; subjects where a uniform law is desirable but not essential go to the Concurrent List.
Changing any List needs a constitutional amendment passed by a special majority of Parliament AND ratified (approved) by half of the State Legislatures (Art 368(2)).

The three-list scheme came from the Government of India Act, 1935 (Federal List 59 items, Provincial List 54, Concurrent List 36). The Concurrent List idea is borrowed from the Australian Constitution.

Art 249 lets Parliament's law-making power be extended without amending the Constitution and without any emergency. So it is counted as a non-federal (unitary, Centre-leaning) feature.

blocks.title: Art 254 — Central law vs State law on a Concurrent List subject

steps.detail: Parliament's law prevails. The State law is void only to the extent of repugnancy (the conflicting part), not wholly.
If the State law was reserved for the President's consideration and got his assent, the State law prevails in that State, even over an earlier Central law on the same subject.
Parliament can later make a law on the same matter and override (add to, amend or repeal) that State law. Parliament is never barred.

items: Example: a State law on adulteration of foodstuffs clashes with a Central law and was never reserved for the President. Result: the Central law prevails.

Overlap between the State List and the Union or Concurrent List is NOT handled by Art 254(1). There the State law fails because of the non-obstante clause of Art 246(1) (the 'notwithstanding anything' words that give Parliament's power priority).

Art 255: if a required recommendation or previous sanction of the Governor or President was not taken, but assent was given later, the Act is still valid. Such requirements are only 'matters of procedure', so missing them does not make the Act void.

head: Doctrine
Meaning
Key cases
rows: Pith and substance (Art 246) — 'true nature' of a law

Look at the true nature ("pith and substance") of the whole law. If it belongs to the enacting legislature's List, the law is valid even if it incidentally touches a subject of another List. Used to decide which List a law really belongs to.

Prafulla Kumar case (1947, Privy Council): Bengal Money Lenders Act valid — in substance about money-lending (State List) though it touched promissory notes (Union List). State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951): Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949 upheld. State of Rajasthan v. G. Chawla (1958): law restricting sound amplifiers upheld. M. Ismail Faruqui (1994): Ayodhya Acquisition Act is 'acquisition of property' (Concurrent List).

A legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly. A law that looks as if it is within the legislature's power, but in reality enters another legislature's field, is void. Also called 'fraud on the Constitution'.
State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952): Bihar Land Reforms Act struck down. K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953): Orissa agricultural income tax law upheld — NOT colourable.
A State law can operate outside the State if there is a sufficient, real (not illusory) connection between the State and the object. Decides the scope of a State's extra-territorial power.
R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla case (1957): a tax on gambling. TISCO case (1958): sales tax. Example: a State taxing an outside company that earns most profits inside the State.

When Parliament and a State both legislate on a Concurrent subject and the laws cannot stand together, Parliament's law prevails. (Some books call this the doctrine of paramountcy: it reconciles conflicting laws where both governments can legislate on the same matter.)
When entries in the Lists seem to conflict, courts first try to read them so both can work; only if that fails does the Union power prevail.

blocks.text: Doctrine of waiver (Basheshar Nath v. CIT, 1959) and doctrine of eclipse belong to Fundamental Rights

items: Only Parliament can make extra-territorial laws (laws working outside India). A State law can reach outside the State only through territorial nexus (a real connection).

Residuary power is with Parliament (Art 248), an idea taken from Canada. Under the 1935 Act it was with the Governor-General; in the USA it is with the States.

Art 249: the Rajya Sabha alone passes the resolution, by two-thirds of members present and voting. It lasts 1 year at a time, and the law lasts 6 more months after it ends. The State can still make laws on the subject.

Art 252: the law applies only to the requesting States, and only Parliament can amend or repeal it. The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 was made under Art 252; the Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982 under Art 253.
A law made during President's Rule continues until the State Legislature changes it. A law made during a National Emergency lapses 6 months after the Emergency ends.

items: They are common to Centre and States; officers hold top posts in both, by turns.

Control is shared. Final control, including the final power to punish an officer, is with the Centre. Day-to-day control is with the State where the officer works.
Each service is one single service with common rights, status and uniform pay scales across India.

Art 312: Parliament creates a new All-India Service by law, only after the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting, declaring it necessary in the national interest.

This Rajya Sabha power (like its power under Art 249) is given to protect the States' interests, because the Rajya Sabha represents the States. The Rajya Sabha cannot allow State legislatures to make laws on Union List subjects.

Compare Art 249: a Rajya Sabha resolution, passed by two-thirds of members present and voting, lets Parliament make laws on a State List subject. The resolution stays in force for one year and can be renewed any number of times, one year at a time. The law stops working six months after the resolution ends. blocks.title: Basic rules
items: Art 265: no tax can be levied or collected except by authority of law. A tax demanded only through an executive order or an office circular is unconstitutional.

The power to levy (impose) and collect a tax is different from the right to keep (appropriate) the money from it. Example: income tax is levied and collected by the Centre, but the money is shared with the States.

Financial relations are mainly in Part XII. Part XII as a whole runs from Art 264 to Art 300A; Laxmikanth treats Art 268 to Art 293 as the Centre–State financial relations. Legislative relations are in Part XI (Art 245 to 255). Administrative relations are also in Part XI (Art 256 to 263).
Art 265 (no tax without law) is in Part XII. Do not confuse: Art 301 (freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse) is in Part XIII, and Art 326 (adult suffrage) is in Part XV.

head: Article
Limit
rows: Tax on professions, trades, callings and employments: at most ₹2,500 per person per year. Original limit ₹250; raised to ₹2,500 by the 60th Amendment (1988). The Punchhi Commission recommended removing this ceiling.

A State cannot tax a supply of goods or services that (a) takes place outside the State, or (b) takes place in the course of import into India or export out of India. Parliament makes the rules to decide when a supply is 'outside the State' or 'in the course of import or export'.
A State cannot tax electricity that is (a) consumed by the Centre or sold to the Centre, or (b) used by the Centre or a railway company to build, maintain or run a railway.

Suppose Parliament has set up an authority to manage an inter-State river or river valley. A State law taxing the water or electricity of that authority is valid only if it is reserved for the President and the President gives assent to it.

head: Feature
Fact
rows: An order of the President (15 September 2016) under Art 279A. Art 279A was inserted by the 101st Amendment.

A constitutional body (created under the Constitution itself). It is a joint forum where the Centre and the States sit together, and is called the 'first constitutional federal body'. It was NOT set up on the Sarkaria Commission's advice (it was the Inter-State Council that was).

The Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance; and the Finance or Taxation Minister (or any other Minister the State nominates) of every State, including Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir
Chosen by the State members from among themselves

The Union Revenue Secretary is the Secretary ex officio (because of holding that post). The Secretariat is in New Delhi. The Chairperson of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) attends every meeting as a permanent invitee but has no vote.

A decision needs at least three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting. The Centre's vote counts as one-third of the votes cast; all States together count as two-thirds. So neither the Centre alone nor the States alone can pass a decision.

A decision of the Council is not invalid merely because (a) a seat was vacant, (b) there was a defect in someone's appointment, or (c) there was a procedural mistake that does not affect the merits of the case

blocks.title: What the Council recommends
items: Which taxes, cesses and surcharges should merge into GST; which goods and services should pay GST and which should be exempted
Model GST laws; principles of levy; how IGST is shared; and place-of-supply rules (rules that decide in which State a supply is taxed)
The turnover limit below which a business is exempt from GST; and GST rates, including floor (minimum) rates with bands

blocks.title: Disputes and institutions
items: Art 279A(11): the GST Council itself sets up a mechanism to settle disputes about its recommendations. It covers three kinds of disputes: (a) Centre vs one or more States; (b) Centre and some States together vs other States; (c) two or more States among themselves. Such disputes do NOT go to the Inter-State Council (Art 263).
GST Network (GSTN): the computer and internet system (IT backbone) used for GST registration, filing returns and paying tax.
GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT): set up under the Central GST (CGST) Act, 2017, to hear appeals in GST disputes.

Union of India v. Mohit Minerals case (2022): the Supreme Court held that GST Council recommendations only have persuasive value (they guide, but need not be followed). They are NOT binding on Parliament and State Legislatures. Reason: Art 246A gives both of them simultaneous power to make GST laws, and Art 279A does not say the recommendations are binding.

Fact

blocks.title: Inter-governmental tax immunities
head: Article
Rule
rows: Union property is exempt from all taxes of States and local bodies, unless Parliament provides otherwise by law. But companies and corporations created by the Centre are NOT exempt, because in law they are separate persons from the Centre.

State property and income are exempt from Union taxes. But Parliament can tax a State's commercial (business) activity. The Centre can also tax the property of local bodies and of companies owned by a State.

head: Emergency

The order lasts till the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ends. The order must be laid before each House of Parliament.

The Centre can direct States to follow canons of financial propriety (rules of proper spending). It can ask States to cut salaries of State employees, and to reserve Money Bills and other financial Bills for the President's consideration.

blocks.text: India's federal system works only if the States also cooperate with each other, not just with the Centre. So the Constitution gives four tools for good relations between States. A fifth tool, the Zonal Councils, was made by an ordinary law of Parliament, not by the Constitution.

items: It is a recommendatory (advisory) body on inter-State, Centre–State and Centre–UT relations. Its recommendations do NOT bind the Union or the States; it cannot enforce anything.

items: Why needed: each State's power stops at its own border, so one State might not recognise another State's acts and records.
Rule: full faith and credit (full acceptance) must be given throughout India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and of every State.
'Public acts' = both legislative and executive acts of a government. 'Public record' = any official book, register or record made by a public servant on duty.
How such acts are proved, and what effect they have, is decided by a law of PARLIAMENT.
Final judgments and orders of CIVIL courts can be executed anywhere in India, without filing a fresh suit. Example: a decree of an AP civil court can be executed on property in Karnataka.
This applies only to civil judgments, NOT criminal ones. A State's courts need not enforce another State's penal (criminal) laws.
Not a tension area in Centre–State relations.

sections.heading: Inter-State trade and commerce (Art 301–307, Part XIII)

head: Article
Rule
rows: Trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India shall be free. Covers BOTH inter-State and intra-State (within one State) trade. Aim: remove border barriers and make India one market. It is not absolute — it is subject to Art 302–305 of Part XIII.
Parliament can restrict this freedom in public interest (example: Essential Commodities Act 1955).
Parliament cannot prefer one State or discriminate between States — except when goods are scarce in some part of India.
A State may tax goods from other States only if similar goods made in that State bear the same tax (no discriminatory tax).
A State may impose reasonable restrictions in public interest, but the bill needs the PRESIDENT's previous sanction (prior permission) before it is introduced.
Laws that create State monopolies (the State alone running a trade, for example by nationalisation) are protected and are not hit by Art 301.
Repealed (removed). It dealt with powers of the old Part B States.
Parliament may appoint an authority to carry out Art 301–304. NO such authority has been appointed so far — the only provision here never used. (In the USA it is the Inter-State Commerce Commission.)

items: Art 263: the PRESIDENT sets up the Inter-State Council — not Parliament. Set up 1990 by Presidential order on Sarkaria's advice — not by amendment, not Rajamannar.
Inter-State Council: chairman PM; Standing Committee chairman Home Minister; decisions by consensus; advisory, not binding.
Zonal Councils: statutory (States Reorganisation Act 1956), NOT under Art 263, NOT constitutional; Home Minister chairs; CMs are vice-chairmen by rotation for one year.
Southern Zonal Council (AP, Telangana) headquarters: Chennai.
Advisers to Zonal Councils (NITI Aayog nominee, Chief Secretaries, Development Commissioners) have NO vote.

Art 262: Parliament can stop the Supreme Court from deciding the water dispute. Since the 2002 amendment, a tribunal award has the force of a Supreme Court decree. But the Supreme Court can still hear appeals by special leave (Art 136).
